arbol_de_trazas.nota: El árbol lo arman el `EjecutorDeEtapas` (corrida y etapa) y el decorador de puertos (una traza por llamada a puerto). **Ninguna etapa emite su propio span** — la observabilidad lo prohíbe y señala al ejecutor como el lugar correcto para el desglose. `campos_censurados > 0` es el registro de decisiones actuando: en una consulta ad-hoc no viaja ni el pedido ni la imagen.

politica.por_que: Las 30 consultas de evaluación se trazan **completas** (el registro de decisiones). No son dato de un tercero: son obras de nuestro propio held-out, versionadas con el ground truth porque son el **instrumento de medición** (el registro de decisiones). Trazarlas enteras cumple las técnicas avanzadas aisladas por medición, la tabla de tokens, costo y la figura y el criterio de costo sin tocar el compromiso de privacidad.

entrada.nota_de_retencion: el registro de decisiones (cierra la pregunta por el ciclo de vida de la corrida purgada): **no se persiste nada de un tercero**. Los bytes de la imagen no se guardan nunca —no hay clave que los active— y el `pedido` solo si `[retencion] pedido = true`. Lo que se vacía son **campos**, y que estaban vaciados queda registrado (la regla de qué se versiona): la corrida conserva su `corrida_id`, su ordinal, sus rankings y sus degradaciones, porque borrarla reasignaría el ordinal y un informe que cita la corrida #1 apuntaría a otra ejecución.

aic:4758.texto:
“What say you to a summer morning?” John Constable wrote of this painting in a letter to a friend. Even after many years living in London, Constable continued to portray the countryside, dear to him from boyhood. Stoke-by-Nayland lies a few miles from his native village of East Bergholt in Suffolk. In this view, he divided the canvas between a brilliant, airy vista toward the hamlet on the left and a shady, tunnel-like country lane leading off to the right. Constable explained in his letter that the painting depicted a speciﬁc time, a morning in “July or August, at eight or nine o’clock, after a slight shower during the night, to enhance the dews in the shadowed part of the picture.” The artist emphasized the abundance of water through his painting technique, ﬂecking the surface with white highlights to create an effect of sparkling wetness. Here, the whole scene appears dewy, with a stream and puddles in the foreground and a central tree that droops from the weight of rainwater, emphasizing the fertile land.
Painted as much with a palette knife as with brushes, Stoke-by-Nayland lacks the ﬁnish of pictures Constable exhibited publicly; it was meant as a full-scale sketch for a work that he never realized. Nonetheless, this canvas seems to capture Constable’s delight in freely scribbling and scraping the image into existence—what it lacks in detail it gains in atmosphere. The roughness of the surface evokes the textures of real landscape, and the coexistence of natural and built elements in the scene embodies an ideal of harmony indicative of Constable’s vision of rural England.
aic:4758.title: Stoke-by-Nayland

aic:97292.texto: Robert Vonnoh was among the first American painters to explore Impressionism. He received his formative artistic training in Boston and headed to Paris in the early 1880s for further instruction. By the late 1880s, Vonnoh had settled in Grez-sur-Loing, a rural area outside of Paris that attracted a growing colony of artists who worked outdoors. Here, using a brilliant palette, broken brushstrokes, and unblended colors, Vonnoh captured the budding vegetation and warming sunlight of a spring day. Intense greens, peaches, and lavenders convey the dappled light and shadows of a winding road at right. The fence posts marking the edge of the yard and white linens hanging from a nearby tree highlight the scene’s domestic setting.
aic:97292.title: Spring in France

cma:122345.texto: Inspired by the native Dutch landscape, Meindert Hobbema specialized in scenes of dense forest growth punctured by winding paths and views toward sunlit clearings that beckon with fertile fields and rustic cottages. Hobbema’s paintings were especially popular among Dutch citizens, who took enormous pride in their land. In addition to nationalistic pride in having recently gained independence from Spain, there was also a profound awareness of the preciousness of land in a low-lying nation, which required dikes, pumps, and constant vigilance to guard against flooding. While the Dutch earned much of their considerable wealth from sea trade, agriculture and livestock were important sources of prosperity.

cma:124078.texto: Corot painted this view of a pond near his home at Ville-d'Avray, just west of Paris, in his late style distinguished by soft, hazy forms and gentle, silvery light. Such paintings merge his lifelong study of nature with nostalgic memories and contrast sharply with the more formal compositions and precisely rendered shapes of his early landscapes. Corot's devotion to the direct study of nature was a major influence on the Impressionists.
cma:124078.title: Pond at Ville-d'Avray

cma:157104.texto: Fellow artist Edouard Manet considered Jongkind the "father of modern landscape painting."
cma:157104.title: The Seine at Bas-Meudon

cma:157104.texto: Although born and trained in Holland, Jongkind spent much of his life painting outdoors in France. In this depiction of Bas-Meudon near Paris, the artist applied paint in small patches of bright color to suggest the intensity of outdoor light. Although typcially finished in the studio from open-air sketches, Jongkind's oil paintings achieve a convincing immediacy that greatly impressed the young Claude Monet. The two met in the early 1860s and spent part of a summer painting together along the coast of Normandy. "From that time he was my real master," Monet later acknowledged, "it was to him that I owe the final education of my eye."
cma:157104.title: The Seine at Bas-Meudon

plan.nota_de_identidad: Clase **1 / 2** (la tabla de identidades), el **híbrido**: se *direcciona* como caché de entradas —eso **es** el reuso del plan al barrer el peso de fusión, cinco corridas de un barrido de `α` reusando un plan— y su contenido es la salida **no determinista** de un LLM. Por eso la regla de que un id determina su contenido no aplica y lo que rige es **escritura única** (la escritura única del plan). lo que no entra en la identidad del plan: `α`, N, la fusión y el `variante_id` **no** son ingredientes. la versión del prompt como ingrediente del plan: el prompt **+ su versión**, el modelo y el muestreo **sí**.
plan.nota_de_pl3: Las **tres** cláusulas van escritas porque son **tres cosas**: que las dos consultas existan, que difieran del pedido crudo (*rewriting*) y que difieran entre sí (lo que distingue *expansion* de *rewriting*). El veredicto viaja adentro para que las tres cláusulas de las consultas del plan se pueda contar **también sobre una ad-hoc**, cuyo pedido el registro de decisiones no deja guardar.
plan.nota_de_pl5: la escritura única del plan: un `plan_id` se escribe **una sola vez**; si ya existe se **lee** y la corrida registra si lo **produjo o lo reusó**. Sin ese registro no habría forma de saber **qué corrida pagó la llamada que la tabla de tokens, costo y la figura cuenta**.

formato.nota: El formato concreto **sigue abierto**: esto es la **cosmética declarada**, no el contrato. El contrato —`[n]` que asigna el renderizador, toda afirmación con dato citando un `fragment_id` recuperado en esta consulta, 100 % de los CC-BY con atribución, español + cita textual en inglés— vive en el código y es el conteo de referencias colgadas, el criterio de atribución, el criterio de idioma y las obligaciones de la cita.

salida.nota_de_idioma: el contrato de la salida citada / el criterio de idioma: la explicación en **español**, el fragmento citado **textual en inglés, sin traducir**. La cita viaja desde `knowledge` hasta acá **sin pasar por el modelo** (el contrato de salida), y las obligaciones de la cita lo verifica byte a byte: si el formateo viviera dentro del prompt, *'textual'* dependería de que el modelo no lo reescriba.

   El uso de colores brillantes y la representación de la luz natural aportan una sensación de vida y movimiento en el paisaje.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “Although born and trained in Holland, Jongkind spent much of his life painting outdoors in France. In this depiction of Bas-Meudon near Paris, the artist applied paint in small patches of bright color to suggest the intensity of outdoor light. Although typcially finished in the studio from open-air sketches, Jongkind's oil paintings achieve a convincing immediacy that greatly impressed the young Claude Monet. The two met in the early 1860s and spent part of a summer painting together along the coast of Normandy. "From that time he was my real master," Monet later acknowledged, "it was to him that I owe the final education of my eye."”
       https://clevelandart.org/art/1993.236 · CC0 1.0

4. **Pond at Ville-d'Avray**
   Jean Baptiste Camille Corot · late 1860s · oil on fabric
   Ficha oficial: https://clevelandart.org/art/1944.80

   La obra presenta formas suaves y una luz plateada y tenue que reflejan una impresión nostálgica y soñadora del paisaje. [1]
   La calidad onírica de la pintura busca reproducir la 'primera impresión' del paisaje, lo que sugiere una atmósfera tranquila y contemplativa más que una escena llena de vida activa. [2]
   La atmósfera suave y difusa transmite serenidad pero menos sensación de vida intensa o movimiento.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “Corot painted this view of a pond near his home at Ville-d'Avray, just west of Paris, in his late style distinguished by soft, hazy forms and gentle, silvery light. Such paintings merge his lifelong study of nature with nostalgic memories and contrast sharply with the more formal compositions and precisely rendered shapes of his early landscapes. Corot's devotion to the direct study of nature was a major influence on the Impressionists.”
       https://clevelandart.org/art/1944.80 · CC0 1.0
   [2] “The dreamlike quality of the painting reflects Corot’s desire to reproduce the “first Impression” of the landscape.”
       https://clevelandart.org/art/1944.80 · CC0 1.0

5. **Stoke-by-Nayland**
   John Constable · 1836 · Oil on canvas · 19th century
   Ficha oficial: https://www.artic.edu/artworks/4758

   La pintura representa una mañana de verano después de una ligera lluvia, con efectos de rocío y humedad que realzan la vitalidad del paisaje. [1]
   El artista usó una técnica que crea efectos de brillo y humedad, con reflejos blancos que simulan el agua y transmiten una sensación de frescura y vida. [1]
   La superficie rugosa y la combinación de elementos naturales y construidos evocan texturas reales y una atmósfera viva y dinámica.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] ““What say you to a summer morning?” John Constable wrote of this painting in a letter to a friend. Even after many years living in London, Constable continued to portray the countryside, dear to him from boyhood. Stoke-by-Nayland lies a few miles from his native village of East Bergholt in Suffolk. In this view, he divided the canvas between a brilliant, airy vista toward the hamlet on the left and a shady, tunnel-like country lane leading off to the right. Constable explained in his letter that the painting depicted a speciﬁc time, a morning in “July or August, at eight or nine o’clock, after a slight shower during the night, to enhance the dews in the shadowed part of the picture.” The artist emphasized the abundance of water through his painting technique, ﬂecking the surface with white highlights to create an effect of sparkling wetness. Here, the whole scene appears dewy, with a stream and puddles in the foreground and a central tree that droops from the weight of rainwater, emphasizing the fertile land.
Painted as much with a palette knife as with brushes, Stoke-by-Nayland lacks the ﬁnish of pictures Constable exhibited publicly; it was meant as a full-scale sketch for a work that he never realized. Nonetheless, this canvas seems to capture Constable’s delight in freely scribbling and scraping the image into existence—what it lacks in detail it gains in atmosphere. The roughness of the surface evokes the textures of real landscape, and the coexistence of natural and built elements in the scene embodies an ideal of harmony indicative of Constable’s vision of rural England.”
       https://www.artic.edu/artworks/4758 · CC BY 4.0
       “Stoke-by-Nayland”, John Constable. Art Institute of Chicago. Texto bajo CC BY 4.0 — https://www.artic.edu/artworks/4758
